issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 21-year-old female whose trauma type is witnessing another person's trauma, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It does not plausibly connect to the other selected cues (blood, crash discussions) or to the rest of the profile unless there were a very specific female-linked circumstance, which is not reflected elsewhere.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Carry Weapon: carry weapon
issues.explanation: 'Carry weapon' is difficult to justify from the rest of the formulation and symptom content. There is no corresponding threat item or appraisal of current interpersonal danger, and the trauma is witnessing rather than direct assault. This strategy therefore appears to address a threat context not represented elsewhere in the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is poorly matched to a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, especially when no memory or trigger item suggests the patient herself was physically injured. This negative appraisal implies direct bodily harm and is inconsistent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Before the accident, Leila had loved the quiet of the forest-the way the air smelled of damp earth and pine, the rhythm of her boots on the trail. At twenty-one, she was one of the youngest foresters in the county, proud of her work marking diseased trees and mapping fire breaks. That changed on a late October afternoon when she crested a ridge and saw the pickup truck swerve off the logging road, flip twice, and land crumpled against a boulder. She was the first to reach the driver. There was blood on the windshield, blood on her hands as she tried to find a pulse she never found. She could still smell it, sometimes-copper and diesel and wet clay-as if it were happening all over again. That smell would hit her without warning, and the memory would surface, but it felt like it belonged to someone else, not to her. She would push it away before she could fully recall what the man's face looked like, but the pushing itself took effort, and she had come to believe that the effort was a sign of something wrong in her.

In the weeks that followed, Leila began to avoid anything that might bring the event to mind. When a coworker mentioned the accident at a team meeting, she excused herself and walked out. She started staying up until two or three in the morning, delaying sleep because she dreaded what her mind might replay in the dark. What frightened her most was the certainty that she had failed-that she should have done more, should have climbed down the embankment faster, should have known first aid well enough to save him. She had acted in ways that went against who she thought she was; she had frozen, and that frozen person felt like a stranger. She used to be happy, but now she was always miserable, and that misery felt like proof that she had become someone else entirely.

Her work suffered. As a forester, she spent her days surrounded by the sights and sounds of the woods, but now she was constantly scanning the environment for signs of threat-a distant engine, a flash of metal between the trees. Every car she saw on the logging road was a car that could crash. Every blood-red berry on a bush made her stomach turn. The scanning was exhausting, but she was certain that if she stopped paying attention, something terrible would happen again, and it would be her fault. She had come to believe that her vigilance was the only thing keeping the world from falling apart, even as it kept her from sleeping, from concentrating, from feeling like herself.

The checking and the avoidance only made the memories more intrusive. When she finally did sleep, she would wake with the smell of diesel in her nostrils and the sense that she had been somewhere she should not have been. The memory felt alien, like a film she had watched rather than a life she had lived, and that alienation made her doubt her own mind. She began to avoid not just the accident site but the entire western section of the forest, rerouting her patrols even though it added two miles to her day. The avoidance made the memory feel more dangerous, and the danger made her scan harder, and the scanning brought the smell back again.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in late January when she found herself standing in the middle of a clearing, unable to move, because she had seen a red truck parked near a trailhead. It was a different truck, a different driver, but her heart had hammered so hard she thought she might pass out. She had walked away without completing her inspection, and that night she had looked at herself in the bathroom mirror and thought, I cannot keep living like this. She was afraid that if she did not find a way out, she would lose her job, lose the one thing that had made her feel competent and whole. She was afraid of what she might become if the misery never lifted. But she was also afraid of what it would mean to stop scanning, to stop checking, to let the memories come fully-because if she let them come, she might have to face the person she had been that afternoon, and she was not sure she could survive that.
